Live capture becomes a worker pool: threads (default 1 = the historical sequential capture, cap 32, refused beyond rather than clamped). Claims CAS-issued from an atomic counter — claims are promises to send, attempts are settled sends; the sequential loop's attempt()<requested check was safe only because one goroutine ran it. Both pauses gate between sends in every worker (same placement as before, so a pause never splits a response). Miss-streak guard: per-worker streak, so a location that never matches stops in the same order of magnitude of requests the sequential guard produced (a global streak ÷ thread count would have cost threads×25 requests on a broken location). Cancellation classifies in the closer — several workers see ctx.Done at once and exactly one task.Stop lands, so the dashboard reads a cancelled capture as stopped. Wire: threads on the capture request; form gains the field with the shared-bound caveat in the hint. Tests: threads=1 never overlaps, threads=4 overlaps and collects every token, threads=33 refused, wide pool never claims one ordinal twice (origin stamps tokens at ACCEPT time — stamping at write time races across overlapping connections and mimics the duplicate-claim defect). Fixed in 49414e6. POST /api/proxy/ca/regenerate mints a fresh CA and installs it, with a Settings button beside import/export behind a confirm dialog carrying Burp's own warning. RegenerateCA reuses generateCAPEM and installs through ImportCA rather than growing a second generator — ImportCA validates before it swaps, so a pair that failed validation leaves the running CA and leaf cache untouched and the caller is told the rotation did not happen. Refuses when it cannot mean anything: with TLS interception off it answers 503 naming the flag rather than minting a CA nothing would use. No key material in the response or the log (subject only); route classified riskDestructive. Verified live on an -intercept-tls console: CA serial 073B527B3B504C31C6660200FE54FC08 -> E6C0C1B13E379A9CA3C2E0E91021177F, different SHA-256 fingerprints, new CA has basicConstraints CA:TRUE pathlen:1, response body contains no PRIVATE KEY block. The decisive check — a leaf minted for an HTTPS origin proxied AFTER the rotation: 'openssl verify -CAfile <current> leaf.pem' -> OK, and the same leaf against the pre-regeneration CA -> 'error 20 ... unable to get local issuer certificate'. So the proxy signs under the new CA and the old one no longer validates what it signs. Go: ca_regenerate_test.go + api_ca_regenerate_test.go; gates green.

Fixed in b27e047. ApplyAll dropped a position whose payload escapePayload refused and built the request from what remained — for a single-position attack that IS the base request, so the attempt went out unmodified and landed in the report among the real sends. NOTE for the record: the plumbing existed but was DEAD when I picked this up — applyAllChecked had no caller (ApplyAll discarded the refusals with 'out, _ :=') while its comment claimed the driver used it. The driver is now actually wired at both sites (the plan loop and the recursive chain): a refused payload records the attempt with the enumerator's own reason (bcheck WireValue, the same text the scanner reports for the same payload at the same point) and NEVER sends the bytes — the same shape the scope guard's refusal already takes. The chain stops after a refusal because nothing was sent, so there is no response to extract the next payload from. Verified: TestAPayloadItsContainerRefusesIsReportedAndTheBaseRequestIsNeverSentInstead runs a real sniper attack at a multipart part's content with payload 'before
--X after' (a CRLF plus this body's own boundary delimiter, which would terminate the part; a bare '--X' is legal and IS spliced verbatim per the sibling test, so this is specifically the refused shape) and asserts nothing reached the sender, Sent=0, Failed=1, and the attempt carries a reason. alice, the part's ORIGINAL value. gofmt/build/vet clean; go test ./internal/intruder ./internal/web green.

Fixed in 3b4c089. The bead's first check mattered: the tool-log record did NOT carry a content type, so a filter matching on something reconstructed would have lied. The fact is now recorded rather than inferred — Entry.Mime holds core.MimeEssence of the response (the same one-line answer Exchange.Mime uses, so a Logger row and a history row can never disagree) supplied by the proxy path, which is where a long engagement's rows come from. NOTE: when I picked this up the filter arm existed but NO caller supplied a MIME, so it could never fire — a decorative control. Wiring the proxy record path is what made it real. Two kinds of 'no type' kept apart: nil = the caller never measured one (never judged), "" = a response that declared none (a measured fact matching no pattern); Record passes nil, RecordMime is for callers that know. EXCLUSION list, not inclusion: burpsy's vocabulary is the open set of essences MimeEssence produces, so an inclusion list would silently refuse every type nobody thought to add. Patterns are type/subtype or type/*; anything else refused with the reason. Verified live proxying a real image/png and text/html origin: no filter -> both captured; mime [image/png] -> /c.png RELAYED http=200 but NOT captured while /d.html captured, filtered_total 1; mime [image/*] -> /f.png not captured, /g.html captured, filtered_total 3; GET returns filter.mime so the choice survives a reload; mime [image] -> 400 'invalid MIME pattern "image": want type/subtype or type/*'. The relayed 200 on refused rows is the point: this is a CAPTURE filter, not a block. Mutate-and-verify: disabling the arm fails with 'a row whose response was image/png was captured, so the exclusion did nothing and the log still fills with images'. Gates green.

Fixed in ce11b60. The bead's honest first question — is the first byte measured at all? — was no, so it is now MEASURED rather than synthesised: ReadResponseHeadTimed takes the instant inside the read at the wire, and the untimed ReadResponseHead became a wrapper over the same parser so the two cannot drift. TTFB is a core.ExchangeDuration, so (Measured, Us) keeps 'nobody timed this' separable from 'this was instant'; only producers that own the response read populate it (the HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 relays), while Repeater, Intruder, the crawler and pre-existing rows leave it Unmeasured. The wire carries ttfb_ms as a POINTER — null, never 0 — because 0 would claim an instantaneous first byte for every exchange nobody timed; the column renders an em dash. The proxy's parity guard forced this to be a DECISION rather than an omission: core.Exchange's field rules refused to pass until TTFB was classified, and it is ruleMayDiffer with the reasoning recorded (the crawler fetches through a client that hands back a finished response and genuinely cannot state a first-byte instant; forcing ruleIdentical would make one producer lie). Verified live through the proxy against two origins built to defeat the old single column, both ~1s total: /slow-head ttfb_ms=1002 duration_ms=1002 (origin took ~1s to START answering) vs /slow-body ttfb_ms=2 duration_ms=1003 (answered at once, BODY took ~1s). One total cannot tell those apart; the pair does. Unit test asserts the MARSHALLED JSON, because that is where the distinction lives (nil *uint64 -> null vs uint64 -> 0). gofmt/build/vet clean; go test across core/httputil/scanner/proxy/web green; tsc + bun test clean.

Fixed in 9db168b. Burp's Token handling, both halves. Padding: the statistical tests can only run over tokens of one length, and WHERE the padding goes changes which byte positions every character and bit test reads, so the mode is none (unchanged default) / start / end with the pad character configurable (Burp's default '0', pre-filled rather than relying on the zero value, which is NUL). Base64-decode before analysing: a base64 token's randomness is in the bytes it encodes, not the alphabet it is written with; order is decode, then pad, then analyse, because padding a base64 string and then decoding it would decode a different string. The padding is REPORTED, not silently applied — tokens_padded, pad_bytes_added and the original length range ride in the report, so a reader of a quoted finding can answer 'how much of this analysis is my own padding?'; base64_decoded says which sample the numbers describe. Refusals never clamps: a token that is not valid base64 while decoding is on is refused NAMING which token (passing it through undecoded would produce a report over a sample half decoded and half not), an unknown pad mode is refused rather than falling back to none, and a pad 'byte' that is not exactly one byte is refused. Verified live: tokens [abcd,ab,a] with no padding -> mode=none tokens_padded=0; pad_mode=start pad_byte=0 -> mode=start tokens_padded=2 pad_bytes_added=5 orig=1..4; base64 tokens with decode off -> base64_decoded=false encoding=base64 (measuring the alphabet), decode on -> base64_decoded=true encoding=raw (measuring the bytes) — the encoding flip is the evidence that decoding changed what was analysed, not just what was labelled. Three refusals each 400 naming the value. Go tests pin pad-start vs pad-end placement, the counts, that the longest token is untouched, that PadNone changes nothing, that decoding analyses the 4 decoded bytes not the 8 encoded characters, and that a non-base64 token is refused by index. Gates green.

Fixed in 6c2a9b8. Intruder was the only whole Burp top-level menu with no counterpart; it is now in the menubar (burpsy · File · Intruder · Repeater · Tools · View · Help) with Burp's item set. The acceptance rule — enabled items do their job, and anything that cannot be honoured is absent or DISABLED WITH A REASON, never a no-op — is met item by item: Start attack 'Choose a stored message id first.' (and the reason is recomputed from the page as the form fills, naming the next missing thing in the order an operator fills it in), Stop 'No attack is running.', Open saved attack 'burpsy has no project file, so a finished attack and its results are not stored on disk to be reopened. Save attack config writes the configuration to a JSON file instead.' — that last one is the honest half: rather than a stub that pretends, the item says what burpsy has instead. Only the mounted page can size an attack, so the page publishes its status and the menubar reads it; the menu asks via a one-shot command carrying a nonce (two identical clicks are two commands, not one ignored repeat). Neither command nor status is persisted, for a sharp reason: a persisted 'start' would fire an attack against a live target on every page load with no click behind it. Save/Load attack config write the whole IntruderConfig, guarded by Record<keyof IntruderConfig, Check> — that guard FIRED while landing this, and the nine fields the page had grown since (manual markers, grep-match list, the nn0n delay variation, retries, baseline) are now carried; a loader that quietly defaulted a field would hand back an attack that reads like the saved one and sends different requests. Verified live in a real browser: 12 menu items with the greyed ones carrying their reasons in the title; after configuring an attack Start flips to enabled; clicking it ran a REAL attack — SENT 5 of 5 planned, COMBINATIONS 5 exact, FAILED 0, ELAPSED 205 ms, mode sniper — and the Results pane rendered its report (the crash an earlier run reported on the stale base did not reproduce). tsc clean; bun test 559 pass (23 new); go build clean.

Fixed in e966085. Burp's Configuration library: named scan configurations the operator saves, clones, renames and deletes, and picks when launching. The shipped presets and the operator's own are ONE list, each row marked shipped or saved — two lists would be two answers to the same question, and an audit resolves a name. A saved configuration is stored as the RESOLVED AuditConfig, one JSON document per name, not a diff against a preset: a diff would silently change meaning whenever its preset changed, and what was saved is what must come back. Zero = every request (the pre-field behaviour, so every existing rule is unaffected); a negative interval is refused at configuration time rather than read as always/never, because 'validate never' is a rule that silently stopped protecting the session. The count is per RULE and advanced once per REQUEST, not per check: the tests caught the per-call version, where a rule's two checks disagreed about which request was due (on request 1 one skipped and the other ran). The counter is not persisted: it is a running cost decision, and restoring it would make a rule's behaviour depend on when the process last stopped; a restart is the safe direction. readFullRequest searched for the exact string "Content-Length:" and read that body. A request framed with Transfer-Encoding: chunked matched neither branch, so the reader returned after the header block: the proxy forwarded a head promising a body it had never read, the origin waited for bytes that would never arrive, and history recorded a bodyless POST. Reproduced live before the fix at 98 bytes in / 53 out. Both framings are now read. A chunked stream is decoded and the head rewritten to Content-Length rather than re-framed, because the intercept hold, match-and-replace pass, editor and record each take one whole byte slice. A short body, a chunk stream that ends before its terminal chunk, and an unparseable chunk size each return the head alone: forwarding a half-read body behind a head claiming it whole is the exact corruption being fixed. Header names fold and chunked may carry parameters, so both lookups are case-insensitive and token-aware (the old exact-case search also dropped a lower-case Content-Length body). Buffered body bounded at 64 MiB, because this reader holds one whole request in memory and a chunk stream can declare any size. Verified against a raw TCP origin reporting the exact forwarded bytes: the same upload that arrived as a 53-byte bodyless head now arrives as 104 bytes, payload decoded and Content-Length correct. Every response was buffered to completion before the client saw any of it. On a response that does not end -- an SSE feed, a long-poll -- httputil's ReadResponseBody copies an unframed body until EOF and EOF never comes, so the client received no bytes at all until the connection's own deadline fired, which it reads as a hung target. Three legs buffered and all three are fixed: the HTTP/1 plaintext path (handleHTTP now hands the request to streamPlainResponse, which owns the upstream connection for the life of the stream, which is why the branch sits before forwardRequest rather than after it), the HTTP/1-over-TLS intercept loop (streamTLSResponse, with the read deadline set on the upstream leg from the policy window), and relayH2Stream, which did io.ReadAll on the response body -- the same defect on the protocol nearly every TLS origin negotiates. The predicate is deliberately not 'is this response frameless': a real event stream is chunk-framed and never sends its terminal chunk, so testing for missing framing classified every genuine SSE feed as ordinary and buffered it. What distinguishes them is whether the framing completes, known only once the read has run. A framed response is never streamed: Match & Replace and the hold are entitled to see the whole message before any of it reaches the client. A streamed response is forwarded live then recorded and is NOT held -- a rule cannot rewrite a byte the client already has. Both record paths gained an alreadyWritten flag rather than a second recording function. The window comes from the same Settings > Network list the sender reads; the proxy had no access to it, so the panel described a list only Repeater obeyed. A negative window is refused rather than clamped. Verified live through a real console against a real h2 SSE origin: first event at +60ms while the origin was still sending, second at +6.01s on release; before the fix both arrived together at the end. Mutation-checked four ways: buffering instead of streaming, the predicate off, the record dropped, and the settings push to the proxy removed or losing the operator's window. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./... green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

An operator who configured Basic or Digest under Settings > Network > Platform authentication got authenticated Repeater sends, authenticated scanner probes, and an UNAUTHENTICATED browser through the proxy -- where most of their traffic is -- while the panel said the rules were stored. The NTLMv2 codec landed in 3fb2ce1 and was unreachable for the traffic that needed it. The same *netauth.Credentials the sender holds is now handed to ProxyConfig, so one set of rules governs every leg. The edit is a header insert at the request head's terminator, not a request rebuild: the proxy relays bytes, and rebuilding one to attach a credential would mean parsing it, re-serialising it, and hoping the round trip is byte-identical for everything the parse did not model. The browser's own Authorization header always wins, case-insensitively. There is no retry, deliberately -- a 401's challenge is learned as each response head arrives so the NEXT request authenticates, across a new connection, because re-sending a request the browser did not ask to repeat against a refusing host is how an account gets locked out. GET /api/network/auth now reports presented_on_proxy beside presented_on_egress, because a Server can be assembled with one leg and not the other. Every intercepted TLS leg opened with InsecureSkipVerify: true and nothing anywhere could turn it off, so an operator comparing two builds of the same app could not tell from burpsy whether the certificate had changed -- a swapped, expired, self-signed or hostname-mismatched certificate was indistinguishable from a good one. Verification now defaults to ON (Burp's default, and the only safe reading of a field whose absence would mean accept anything), with two escape hatches replacing the unconditional skip: a custom CA bundle that keeps verification on while trusting one more issuer, and verify:false as the deliberate opt-out for a self-signed lab target. Both live in NetworkSettings, so the setting is live, persisted and API-edited and the SAME edit reaches the sender and the proxy; the sender's TLSVerify is the fallback for a sender built without network settings applied. alpn.Dialer gained RootCAs and MinVersion, which is where the two legs would otherwise have drifted. A protocol floor below TLS 1.0 is refused rather than clamped, and a CA bundle that will not parse is reported when it is configured rather than at a later handshake. Verified live through a real console against a real self-signed origin: REFUSED with verification on, 200 after the operator's own CA was added with verification still on, 200 with verification explicitly off, each set through the console's API -- before the change the first case returned 200 silently. A login or SSO flow that sets a cookie on its 302 arrived at the destination unauthenticated: the redirect was followed, the cookie was not sent, and the destination returned its login page, which reads as an application failure rather than a missing cookie. Burp exposes the fix as a setting; burpsy had the absence documented, so nothing on screen was wrong. ReplayCookies defaults OFF unlike a browser's, because burpsy sends what an operator wrote and a target-set credential is not something they asked to send. Each hop's Set-Cookie is absorbed and the next hop carries it, scoped to that hop's own authority and Path; a hop that already carries a Cookie header keeps it. The jar is the SESSION coordinator rather than a second store, behind a two-method interface because internal/session imports internal/sender, and it takes the Set-Cookie values rather than response bytes. A real bug the unit tests could not see: repeaterSendOptions.redirectPolicy rebuilt RedirectSettings field by field on a per-send mode override, so ReplayCookies dropped to false -- the console showed the setting ON, the operator sent with 'always', and no cookie was replayed, with every sender test green because they attach their own jar. The rebuild is now copy-and-replace-one-field. Live through a real console against a real login flow: replay off, the hop request carries no Cookie and the destination answers LOGIN PAGE; replay on, the same request carries Cookie: session=real-session-value and the destination answers DASHBOARD. Mutation-checked six ways including removing the absorb, removing the apply, letting the jar replace the operator's own header, never attaching the session jar, and dropping the hop's Path. Split out of mr83, which stays open for the DNS family preference and the global SOCKS carrier. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./... green, tsc clean, bun test:lib 711/0, check:tokens green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

A dual-stack target behind IPv4-only routing can resolve to an AAAA first, and burpsy dialled the unreachable address, so a request took the connect timeout to fail on a host that was reachable all along; there was no setting that fixed it and the only workaround was the per-hostname override table. Burp's answer is the resolution-address preference (settings/network/dns.html:49-65), 'because routing restrictions may permit only one family'. Resolution.Family is system/ipv4/ipv6, applied on BOTH dial paths -- the raw sender and the typed transport Repeater uses, because two paths that disagreed would be a Repeater send that reached an IPv6-only host and a scanner probe that did not. It is a filter over the resolver's answer rather than a resolver rewrite: a per-family query can be answered differently by a split-horizon resolver than a filtered answer to the question the operator asked, and the engagement's own DNS is what knows. An override is never filtered, because the operator named an address and substituting another is worse than the defect. System costs no lookup, so an ordinary send pays nothing for a preference nobody set. A family with no address is a named failure pointing at the field to change. The live pass could not demonstrate the defect and the reason is recorded in the test: this host has no IPv6 route, so an AAAA dial fails in 0.00s instead of timing out, and both family=system and family=ipv4 answered 200 in under 10ms against an IPv4-only listener. The selection is proved through a Lookup seam answering with both families, IPv6 first, against a real IPv4 listener: the send reaches the listener and the listener sees the connection. Mutation-checked three ways: a no-op filter, system treated as a filter, and removing the preference from the typed transport -- the third survived the first round of tests and is why the two-family seam exists. Split out of mr83, which stays open for the global SOCKS carrier. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./... green with the test cache cleared, tsc clean, bun test:lib 711/0, check:tokens green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

A blind CONNECT tunnel has no request bytes to record and the proxy builds that row with no Request, but the message store's ids are a dense counter from ZERO, so 0 is the first request the project ever captured and exchangeView emitted that zero unconditionally. The UI read it as 'this row's request is message 0' and the detail pane rendered the project's first request under the label Request for a tunnel that has none -- another exchange's bytes, with nothing marking it. That is evidence corruption, and Burp's own account agrees the absence is the honest state (map_root.tsv:10859: pass-through connections have no details about requests or responses available in the Proxy history). The fix is in the model: core.Exchange.Request is now a *MsgId mirroring Response, which has always been a pointer for the same reason -- a bare MsgId cannot say 'no request' because its zero value IS a real request, so the distinction was unrepresentable anywhere. core.Occurrence, which mirrors the same pair for finding attribution, changed with it. Four sites that silently read the zero as an id are fixed: AddExchange indexed a request-less row under byRequest[0] (Restore could reintroduce it), the variant resolver returned message 0 as the ORIGINAL reading of a row with no request, and api_search scanned ex.Request unguarded -- the same defect reached through search, its response half already having the guard the request half lacked. Two limitations stated rather than hidden: the durable store's request column is NOT NULL and SQLite cannot relax that with ALTER TABLE, so a request-less row persists as 0 and Restore normalises it only when message 0 is absent from the restored set; and about 200 construction sites were converted mechanically using the compiler as an oracle, the only judgement calls being the four above. On the UI side fetchRaw takes number|null and REFUSES with a message naming the reason rather than fetching message 0, and a context-menu plugin is handed message: undefined. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./... green with the test cache cleared, tsc clean, bun test:lib 711/0 plus 4 new, check:tokens green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.
