The Parallel group is now a synchronized send, not fan-out. Every member
dials its own connection and writes its request minus the final byte
(sender.SendSynchronized, new); the orchestrator collects one ready signal
per member — a dial failure counts as an arrival, so one dead port cannot
hang the group — then closes the release channel and every held byte goes
out together. HTTP/1 is pinned for the whole send (ProtocolPreferenceHTTP1,
alpn egress offer excludes h2): there is no "final byte of the raw" once
the h2 path frames it, and the honest h2 equivalent is the single-packet
attack, a separate mechanism. The pin is visible in each result's protocol.

The response pane part of the bead is landed too: results are ranked by the
moment their response's first byte was read (ties by tab order) and the
ordinal ships as `arrival` on Parallel items only — 0/absent for a member
that never answered and for the sequence modes, whose order is tab order by
construction. The UI group-outcome table gains the "Arrived" column (#n)
for parallel sends.

Honest limits, stated rather than papered over:
- Cross-member arrival ORDER is not asserted by any test. With one live
  member, tab order and wire order coincide, so an ordering assertion
  would be vacuous; a multi-member wire-timing double was measured this
  session as unreliable on loopback (three handler goroutines' wake
  order masquerading as the wire). The hold itself IS mutation-checked at
  the sender level: removing the barrier fails the test with the final
  byte queued at the readiness signal, and a cancelled hold returns the
  cancellation error instead of hanging teardown.
- The bundle commit at 6c62d5c already carries this page change (it was
  built from the shared tree); rebuilding at 43a53dc is byte-identical,
  so no separate dist commit exists for ajp6.

Burp's SOCKS setting is a global TCP layer (settings/network/connections.html:177-199): every outbound connection, including requests to upstream HTTP proxies, goes through the SOCKS proxy, with per-host bypasses and a remote-DNS choice. burpsy's model makes proxy KIND part of each destination rule and the policy returns exactly one proxy per address, so there was no layer beneath an HTTP upstream proxy -- an operator had to choose one and lose the other. The layering is a dial concern rather than a rule-editor one: a rule answers which proxy carries this host and a carrier answers what opens the socket to reach that proxy. A carrier carries a DIRECT destination (Burp says every connection), a proxied one, and a SOCKS-rule one, and exempts its own authority host AND port so the hop cannot dial itself; a host-only exemption made the layer silently do nothing for a dev-box operator, which the tests now pin. net.Dialer has no overridable dial field, so a dialer 'carrying' a carrier silently ignores it -- which is why the carrier is a dial FUNCTION applied at the one seam every connection opens through. A live pass found the routing bug the whole unit suite missed: every dial site read the carrier, the panel reported it configured, and the connection still went out direct, because Proxy.DialContext's KindDirect arm opened a bare net.Dialer and an operator who sets a SOCKS layer with no HTTP proxy has a policy resolving everything to Direct. One line in that arm is the feature, and TestADirectPolicyStillCarries is the regression that names it. The carrier is one instance shared by the sender, the proxy listener and the console, carried on SenderConfig at construction because the transport's client captures it then. An HTTPS upstream proxy is NOT carried -- crypto/tls has no dialer field to replace -- and the server reports that in the carrier's limits so the panel says 'Not carried' rather than the setting looking complete. Persisted beside the policy in its own settings row, restored FATAL on refusal. Verified live through a real console: with a carrier configured the SOCKS hop saw the connection and the origin saw none. Mutation-checked three ways plus the Direct arm. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./... green with the test cache cleared, tsc clean, bun test:lib 715/0, check:tokens green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

Burp's Copy other payload exists so two parameters can be held identical while the Cluster bomb varies the rest -- the password and its confirmation case Burp names explicitly. burpsy refused it outside pitchfork, and the refusal was correct: cluster bomb's mixed-radix Fill advances each position's set at a rate that depends on that position's place in the radix system, so a copy stepped by its own ordinal coincided with its source on some requests and diverged on the rest. The test added here measures it -- 60 of 75 requests mismatched, which is 'right most of the time', the worst possible disguise for a correctness bug. The fix is small and exact: Fill already decodes each position's digit as (i/weight_j) % len_j, so a copied position takes the SOURCE's digit at the same ordinal, with the weights computed once per Fill so twenty positions decode twenty digits rather than four hundred. The engine needed no change -- Slot already carries Set and Payload and engine.go reads setBytes[Set][Payload], so a copy is a slot naming its source's set with the source's own ordinal. Pitchfork takes the same path and stays exact for a different reason (one ordinal, not one per radix digit). Sniper and battering ram remain refused, and the message now says why -- they advance ONE set across every position, so 'another position's payload' has no per-position meaning to copy from; the old message blamed cluster bomb, which is no longer true and would have been a lie in the refusal itself. A copy naming a forward, self or out-of-range position is still refused rather than clamped, because a copy that silently resolved elsewhere produces requests whose two 'identical' fields differ. The UI hint no longer says 'Pitchfork only'. Mutation-checked: restoring the own-ordinal copy fails both copy tests. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./... green with the test cache cleared, tsc clean, bun test:lib 715/0, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

Burp's Character frobber and burpsy's CharacterBlocks are two generators, and the close reason that named them together ('character blocks/frobber') is what made the absence look delivered. CharacterBlocks cycles an alphabet to fill repeated blocks of a chosen LENGTH -- alphabet, MinLen/MaxLen/Step, and no input value to vary. Burp's Character frobber 'modifies the value of each character position of an input' and increments one character at a time, and its input is the operator's CURRENT value. Character-by-character mutation of a session token is how an operator finds which position an authorization check or a parser depends on; without it the token can only be mutated wholesale, which cannot separate 'the signature covers all of it' from 'the signature covers the first ten characters'. Three decisions are named in the code. Position-major, so one position is walked across the whole alphabet before moving on and the first divergence from the valid token surfaces in the first few payloads. Characters rather than bytes, so a multi-byte character is one position -- the mutation that delegates the frobber to the blocks generator reports FIVE positions for the two-character base 'e-acute snowman' and splits the snowman in half, which is the conflation made concrete. And the base's own character is emitted first where the alphabet contains it, so an operator can tell whether a position matters; where the alphabet lacks that character, no payload is the base and none is manufactured, because claiming an unperturbed position that was perturbed is the same overclaim as a copy that matches most requests. An empty alphabet defaults to printable ASCII rather than refusing (that is what a token's characters are); an empty base is refused and names the base, because there is nothing to increment. The console label read 'Character blocks (frobber)' on a menu item that WAS the blocks generator; it now reads 'Character blocks' with 'Character frobber' as its own entry and its own fields. The two stale doc claims are corrected so the generators stop sharing a name in the close reasons as well as on screen. Mutation-checked both directions: delegating to the blocks generator fails 3 of 8 tests, and the character-major swap passes every test except the ordering assertion -- which is therefore the only defence of the order. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/intruder + internal/web green, tsc clean, bun test:lib 715/0, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

The auto-pause ENGINE shipped complete with 8f2 -- the predicate, appears/missing mode, simple-vs-regex, case sensitivity, a 400 for an uncompilable expression, an in-flight response collected whole, an attack-level auto_paused counter, and the auto_pause wire field. Every claim about the engine was true. The close reason never said whether an operator could turn it on, and they could not: grep auto_pause in intruder.tsx matched nothing and the launch body was built without the field, so the only way to halt a spray was the manual pause, which requires watching the attack. A capability an operator cannot reach is the same gap as one that does not exist, and the 8f2 reason reads as though it were delivered. This change is only the four controls that reach the engine. The block is sent only when the switch is on AND at least one expression is typed, the same omission rule every other optional field follows, because an absent field and an empty expression list must not be two wire shapes for 'I did not choose'. The server reads an empty list as unconfigured (NewAutoPause returns nil, nil), which is what makes the omission honest, and a test pins the two by running both and comparing. The switch decides only whether the block is SENT; the expressions and mode are the attack's own settings, so toggling off and on must find the list intact. An uncompilable expression is surfaced NEXT TO THE EXPRESSIONS rather than only as a toast: the server answers 400, and a toast after a launch that visibly did nothing is the wrong place when the operator's next action is to edit the expression. The re-homing is narrow on purpose -- only a 400 whose body names auto-pause or an expression, because every other 400 belongs to something else in the form. Five config-file tests now carry the block with NON-default values, since defaults survive almost any bug; the round-trip that failed is the one fmxv's settings had. Two notes learned from writing the tests wrong first: the missing-mode test originally used a reflecting target and expected a mid-run pause, which CANNOT work because Control.Pause blocks until resumed, so a mid-run fire leaves the handler waiting and the assertions never run -- it now fires on the last request. And the mode inversion is pinned by a PAIR, because either test alone passes against a server treating missing as always-true; the mutation check confirms it is caught. Verified live in headless Chromium: checkbox present, off by default, expressions hidden while off, all four controls appearing when enabled, mode offering exactly appears/missing, field reporting its count, plus a screenshot and zero axe-core violations in the enabled state. The only console errors are a missing proxy CA file and a crawler endpoint, neither touched here. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test green, tsc clean, bun test:lib 715/0, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

api_config.go was honest and the UI discarded the answer. configIncludedSections holds 4 entries, configOmittedSections holds 10, and the bundle carries a configCoverage that travels inside the bundle so the file is self-describing, with Partial derived from Omitted so it cannot claim completeness while omissions exist. The modal said, in full, 'Scope, intercept rules and session handling rules are affected' -- three of the four carried sections, omitting uninteresting_headers which IS carried, and saying nothing about the ten settings the export never carried. An operator migrating a project or keeping a configuration record read a partial transfer as a complete one. Two defects, and the second is why the first was not merely untidy. The sentence was a hand-written list, and a hand-written list drifts -- it had already drifted from the server. The fix derives the applied sections from what the server reports applying, so there is nothing left to drift, including the section the old text got wrong in the OTHER direction (a bundle carrying only header lists was described as affecting scope, intercept and session rules while the one thing that moved went unmentioned). And the coverage is read out of the FILE, not the import response, because that split is deliberate on the server: 'a bundle's own account of what it carries is evidence about the file, not an instruction to the importer' (configBundle.Coverage's doc). The distinction the modal now turns on: a bundle with no coverage block has told us nothing about its coverage, which is NOT the same as having told us it carries everything. readBundleCoverage therefore returns undefined rather than {partial:false, omitted:[]}, and the modal says the file does not say what it can carry. A failed import leaves it undefined for the same reason -- nothing applied is a fact, coverage never read is an absence of information -- and collapsing those two is the bug this bead exists to fix, so it is collapsed nowhere. A hand-edited file with a non-string in omitted renders only the strings rather than showing '42' as a setting name. Verified live on both branches against a console started by ui-live.sh: importing a real export reports all 10 omitted settings by name, labels the transfer partial, and lists 'uninteresting headers' among the applied; importing a hand-written bundle with no coverage block gives the unknown-coverage wording, no invented omissions, and no claim of a known-partial transfer it cannot justify. 12 tests, mutation-checked both directions (collapsing unknown to empty fails one case; dropping uninteresting_headers fails two). go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/web green, tsc clean, bun test:lib 730/0, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

A task's detail pane answers 'what did that scan actually find?', and it was answering with the last 20 project findings -- another scan's, a collaborator's, a manual recording -- with the task's name in the header. Burp scopes every one of these tabs to the selected task (running-scans/results/index.html:39-62). Two failure modes, bad in opposite directions: (1) a clean task shows findings, because a scan that found nothing displayed other runs' findings under its own name; (2) a busy task is under-reported, because past 20 project findings this task's own older ones were dropped by the slice while newer ones it never raised were shown. Either way the pane attributes work to the wrong run, which this project treats as worse than an absent panel. The data was already there and the console could not see it: api_capture.go sends task_id on every FindingDetail ('the run that produced this finding'), but types.attack.ts's FindingDetail did not declare it, so the pane could not have asked even if it wanted to. It is declared now, and the scoping lives in a tested module rather than a filter inline in the component -- a filter that returns its input unchanged looks exactly like one that scopes it, which is why this survived a close. Scoping happens BEFORE the 20-cap, and that ordering is the second failure mode's whole defence: capping first lets a busy neighbouring task consume the budget and push this task's older findings out of its own pane. The pane now also says how many it left out, because a cap that reads as a total is the same defect one level up. A finding with no task_id -- a manual recording, an imported collaborator result -- belongs to no run and is excluded from every task's pane; that is a real loss and the right one, since attributing an untracked finding to the scan the operator is looking at is the failure this fixes, and the Issues page still carries every finding including those. The other three panels in the same pane are labelled 'Project-wide' rather than scoped, the honest option this bead names, and it costs a heading. They cannot be scoped without server work that does not exist: Sources is a dashboard-level histogram with no task dimension (api_dashboard.go), CoverageSummary is {label,unit,work_unit,breakdown} with no task id, and ToolLogRow carries no task_id either -- so an Intruder payload's row in a crawl's pane is a misattribution the operator cannot see through. Labelling says what they are; per-task accounting is a different change and is not smuggled in here. Verified live on a console started by ui-live.sh with the project feed forced to hold three findings belonging to OTHER tasks: the pane shows none of them and reads 'This task recorded no issues -- Nothing was raised against this run. The Issues page carries every finding in the project, including the ones this task did not raise.' The previous bundle at HEAD has no such state, so the same fixture would have listed all three. 8 tests, mutation-checked both ways: removing the filter fails 4, capping before scoping fails 2 (the ordering test is the only defence of the ordering). go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/web green, tsc clean, bun test:lib 738/0, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

BurpStatusesNotModelled said 'there is no light-active pass' three times while audit_engine.go had implemented one since 7bkj, both in internal/scanner. The three rows are now true, and the truth is narrower than either old sentence: the light tier IS here (auditRun.lightAudit counts CLEAN same-(kind, host) points across a run and, from the Nth, declines the rest of that type on that host), but what does not exist is a light PASS an item is dispatched into. So LIGHT_AUDITING has no window (an item is auditing and the tier takes a skip decision inside it), LIGHT_AUDITED has no state (a declined point is counted in the item's skipped total and the item still finishes in the ordinary audited state), and NOT_LIGHT_AUDITED describes no disposition (a point either runs or is declined for repetition, both visible on the item that raised it). SKIPPED_DUE_TO_REPETITIVE_BEHAVIOUR moves OUT of the not-modelled list entirely -- it claimed 'there is no repetitive-response detector' while the engine skips points as repetitive. It is the one row whose status genuinely changed, and the modelled count is derived (BurpAuditItemStatusCount - len(NotModelled)), so it rises from 6 to 7 with no arithmetic to keep in step. The table's doc comment now says what the engine DOES with the repetitive rule, so a reader who came for that row finds an explanation rather than an absence. Why this was worth more than a stale comment: the table is the project's own disclosure of what it cannot do, so that an absent capability is never discovered by surprise. A table that denies a capability the engine has is worse than no table -- a reader just wronged about light auditing has no reason to believe the rows about selection or parameter types either. That is why every other row was re-checked rather than the three patched. The table can no longer go stale quietly: four tests check it against the engine -- the doc comment's stated count must equal the row count (the prose is what a reader believes, and a count disagreeing with the rows beneath it is the same defect as a row disagreeing with the engine); every row must give a reason and a stub-length one fails; the three light rows must not claim the tier is absent; and the repetitive row must not be listed while the engine skips for it. The third item: the audit-queue page reduced the retained per-item evidence to six state totals. All of it was already on the wire -- the endpoint hands out scanner.AuditItem wholesale, carrying StepsPlanned, StepsDone, UnitsPlanned, Checks, the three point counts, PointKinds and both timestamps -- but AuditItemRow in the client declared almost none of it, so the page could not render what it was being sent. Those fields are declared now, and Progress / Points / Timing are columns, because a partial audit is diagnosed FROM THE TABLE: the question is which items stopped early and how far they got, which needs every row's number visible at once. Two distinctions the engine's comments insist on are kept and tested: a zero plan reads 'not planned' not 0% (StepsPlanned is zero for an item refused BEFORE planning, a different fact from a plan of length zero that ran), and the percentage is not clamped (a plan grows when a breaker opens, and a clamped 100% hides the denominator moving). Enumerated points and points dropped at the per-request ceiling stay two numbers. Verified live on a console from ui-live.sh with a queue holding one item stopped after 2 of 5 steps, one refused before planning and one complete: the rows read '2/5 steps (40%)' with '9 +3 at limit' points, 'not planned', and '8/8 steps (100%)'. 14 tests across both halves, mutation-checked: folding the empty plan into 0% fails 2, clamping to 100% fails the over-planned case. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./... green with the cache cleared, tsc clean, bun test:lib 748/0, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

All three items, and all three were the same shape: the data is retained and the operator-facing layer drops it. 1. Per-item cancel (a0e4122's sibling commit): Burp's audit-item context menu has offered Cancel since running-scans/results/audit-items/index.html:102-115 and the queue had no way to stop one item. The alternatives were waiting for a slow or heavily-guarded URL to exhaust its own bounds (holding a slot and a thread throughout) or disabling the enclosing live task, which stops every item including the ones that were fine. POST /api/scanner/audit-items/{id}/cancel stops one queued item and nothing else, and is NOT routed through runAudit because it sends nothing -- the route manifest records it as riskLocal where its sibling {id}/again is riskAttack, so an unattended caller is not asked to confirm the one queue action that cannot touch the target. ItemStateCancelled is a NINTH state rather than a flavour of ItemStateBounded, and that is the point: bounded says the target was too expensive, cancelled says a person stopped it, and folding one into the other reports a decision as a budget. Burp has CANCELLED for exactly this reason. It is terminal and NOT a completed audit, so 'how much of this queue finished' keeps counting only work that finished. The cancel is recorded and read at the engine's gate inside auditItem (so both AuditWithin and AuditMultiple get it) rather than applied to work in flight, because there is no per-item context to abandon a dispatched probe with and a half-sent request counted as complete is worse than a late cancel. A refused cancel changes NOTHING, which is asserted rather than assumed -- my first test asserted the opposite, which would have made the gate stop an audit already in flight. 2. Issues carry time and source (f44e46e, 2f2fc27, f54ca57): the view had task_id but not the finding's timestamp, and no source. Both were knowable -- FindingStore.Add has stamped Timestamp since the beginning and TaskID distinguishes a run from a person -- so the wire shape was the only thing missing, which is the same defect the Params field's own comment records ('the store kept the set, the console rendered it, the test asserted it, and the wire shape in between silently dropped it'). Source is derived rather than stored and deliberately has TWO values: there is no provenance field on core.Finding, and guessing BCheck-vs-native from the check name would put an unverifiable claim in a column an operator filters on. The console gains a scan/manual label and a relative age per row, plus a source facet whose empty value means all, and a finding with no timestamp renders as an em dash rather than a date -- new Date(0) is a perfectly good date, which is exactly the problem. 3. A single finding reports with its evidence (a0e4122): GET /api/report/finding/{id} carries the same row the scan-wide export produces plus the request and response behind each evidence entry. Nothing new is stored. Three decisions, each the wrong answer first: JSON only (a second HTML renderer for one finding, and a SARIF rendering of a single result is a shape no tool consumes, is decoration not evidence); the scan-wide exports keep carrying no bytes (thousands of rows and their bodies would make the document unusable, and that constraint is why this path exists, so a test pins it); and ONE row builder extracted so the two exports cannot describe a finding differently, which the old inline comment records having already got wrong once. The zero-id bug this surfaced would have made the FIRST message's evidence vanish: request_msg_id had omitempty and these ids count from zero, so 0 is the first message the project ever captured. Explicit has_request/has_response flags now exist because a zero cannot say whether a message exists. A second honesty fix came from the same work: findingEvidence skipped an entire entry when the exchange could not resolve, so an evicted capture produced a report claiming the finding had been seen nowhere -- the convenience took the evidence with it. Unreadable bytes are counted in messages_omitted rather than dropped, because a report that silently omits half its evidence reads as 'there was no request', which is a claim about the target rather than about the capture. 31 tests across the three items, mutation-checked throughout. Verified live in headless Chromium on a ui-live.sh console: a task's pane shows none of three other-run findings and reads 'This task recorded no issues'; issue rows read 'scan just now', 'manual --' and 'scan 3h ago' with no 1970 anywhere and the Manual facet narrowing 9 items to 3; the single-finding document for a real finding carries 2 messages whose first is the actual captured request, while the scan-wide export carries none. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/scanner + internal/web + internal/report green, tsc clean, bun test:lib 755/0, e2e-go.sh 24/24. One full-suite note: internal/blindxss's TestCaptureThroughRealBrowser timed out on its 15s browser-callback deadline in the run where eight packages competed for CPU; it passes at HEAD in a pristine worktree under the same eight-way load and twice in isolation, so it is a real-browser timing flake in an untouched package, not a regression.

All four items addressed; two shipped as fixes and two shipped as the honest option each was given. 1. Rules combine with AND (75ff80d). Burp's proxy.html:246-268 gives every rule a boolean operator and folds left to right; the enabled list was first-matching-rule-wins, so a conjunction could not be written at all -- 'hold host A AND path /admin' is two rules behaving as a disjunction, which means over-holding or one brittle rule enumerating both facts in one matcher, and it is the most-written interception rule after 'hold on this host'. The default is OR, which is what every pre-existing list evaluates as, so the fold reproduces the old behaviour exactly and adding the column changes nothing until an operator opts in; an unrecognised operator reads as OR for the same reason the action parser does. Two semantics the tests pin because a fold gets them wrong: an AND cannot be rescued by an OR below it, and AND on the FIRST rule is ignored rather than refused (nothing above it to combine with, and the rest of the list must keep working). A near-miss worth recording: SetRules rebuilds every rule field by field and the first version forgot Op on the literal branch -- the field existed, decoded, stored, and was dropped on the way in, the same shape as the Params field whose own comment says the wire shape silently dropped it. 2. Listener filter, same commit. Burp's filter-settings.html:109-116; the column rendered and could not be filtered, and tyeo was closed as a duplicate of mr4p whose close reason implemented only the IP column, so it was closed without ever being built. A comma-separated field normalised like the extension lists. The one rule extracted because it fails quietly: a non-numeric segment is DROPPED, not coerced to 0 -- 0 is what a Repeater/Intruder/crawl row carries, so coercing 'abc' to 0 would show exactly the traffic the operator did not ask for. 0 is not offered as a choice because it is not a port. 3. Parameterized renamed, NOT fixed, and that is the bead's own second option. The label now reads 'Requests with query parameters' and the hint says which half is measured, why a history row cannot see the other, and that the Search box does read bytes. The count -- the correct fix -- is filed as 7py5 because it cannot be done where the filter runs: a history row is an index entry with no request body and core.Exchange has no request Content-Type (its Mime is the RESPONSE's), so per-row computation means reading every request body to classify a list entry, the exact cost the history/message split exists to prevent. The JS half was written, tested, and DELETED rather than committed unused; 7py5 records the rules, the unexamined-is-not-parameterless case being what decides whether the eventual fix is honest or merely wider. 4. Newline corrections on an edited forward, same commit as 1. Burp can add a missing blank line after the headers and strip trailing newlines from a urlencoded body on an EDITED request (proxy.html:273-292); neither existed and Content-Length was already fixed, which changes no newline bytes. Two switches because they are two defects with two symptoms and fixing one does not fix the other; both apply only to an edited message, since untouched traffic came off the wire and is well-formed by construction. The trailing-newline fix is scoped to urlencoded/multipart because a trailing newline in JSON is meaningful inside a string. Content-Length is recomputed after every body change. Restoring the blank line needed a header-block scan because both obvious guesses are wrong in a way that matters -- 'last CRLF' truncates the body by two bytes and 'first CRLF' throws the headers away -- so it walks the lines and asks what each one is, and refuses a message with no CRLF rather than inventing a boundary. A bodiless header block does get its terminator, because that is what makes it forwardable. The setting is an engine setting with its own GET/PUT rather than a per-forward argument, for the reason fixContentLength is not on the route: an operator sets it once, and threading it through Forward would put a setting on every call site that could forget it; GET reads back what is in force because a checkbox showing the defaults while a plugin has set one is a control lying about what it is doing. 27 tests across the three shipped items, mutation-checked: dropping the operator from the fold fails 4, dropping Op in SetRules fails 3, not applying the correction fails the wiring test, trimming non-urlencoded bodies fails the JSON case, and coercing a bad listener segment to 0 fails the coercion case. That last group includes a test added only after a mutation exposed the gap -- every other newline test called Apply directly, so removing the call from Forward passed all of them until one exercised Forward's own bytes through held.Wait. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/intercept + internal/proxy + internal/web green, tsc clean, bun test:lib 761/0, e2e-go.sh 24/24. One caveat: the committed dist/app.js is deliberately not rebuilt, because HEAD's history.tsx carries a three-argument useHistory that only compiles against a data.ts change another session has not committed; a bundle built now would either fail or absorb their uncommitted work.

The correct fix for 80tg item 3, which shipped the rename and filed this. The History 'Parameterized requests' filter counted the query string alone, so every body-only parameterized request was classified unparameterized and dropped: a JSON API POST with a body and no query string, a multipart upload, an XML API call. Those are exactly the requests an operator filters to parameterized traffic in order to find, so the filter did not mean what its name said. The count is computed at the capture seam -- core.RequestParameterCount, called from Capture.Record alongside Mime and RequestFingerprint, for the same reason. A history row is an index entry and carries no request body, so a consumer that wanted this would have to read the bytes back, the cost the history/message split exists to prevent (internal/web/AGENTS.md: 'a list endpoint serves index rows and never resolves message payloads'). A COUNT travels on the row; a body never does. Burp's semantics: SHOW_ONLY_PARAMETERIZED_REQUESTS accepts HttpParameterType.URL OR HttpParameterType.BODY (Zb2y.java:270-273,450-455). So the count is the query string's plus a form body's, and a multipart body's parts are counted by name -- a file part counts, because filename= names it. A bare ?debug with no value is a parameter; an empty segment between separators is not. The load-bearing decision: a body the counter cannot parse -- JSON, XML, anything not name/value -- is counted as ONE, not zero. Reporting zero would tell an operator a request has no parameters when nobody examined it, and a filter that hides requests it could not read reports a clean answer about a request nobody read. It is one and not a guess at how many, because nobody knows and a bigger number would be a claim this function has no basis for. Which makes 0 a weaker claim than it looks, and the column says so: 0 means 'certainly no parameters' and -1 means 'this row predates the count'. That is why the column is NULLABLE rather than NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 like its siblings -- for an unmeasured duration a legacy zero is the honest reading, but for this one it would be a claim no build ever made. A legacy row reads back as -1, the filter KEEPS it, and the hint under the control says how many rows were kept because they were never examined. Dropping a -1 instead would be the filter reporting a verdict on requests it has no information about. The 'Query' table column stays 'Query' and says why: it is the query-string count read off the path, the only half visible without the body. Calling it 'Params' would put a number beside the filter that disagrees with it. The proxy's parity guard required a rule for the new field and was right to: it made explicit what I had left implicit. ruleMayDiffer, for the same reason as RequestFP beside it -- the count comes from the raw request bytes, and the proxy relays them verbatim while the crawler's sender re-renders what it parsed. The parity fixture carries no body so both legs count 0 and ruleIdentical would hold vacuously. 20 tests across four layers, mutation-checked: the pre-fix query-only count fails 6, and reporting an unreadable body as zero fails exactly the JSON, XML and no-Content-Type cases plus the unexamined test -- the overclaim this projection exists to prevent. A legacy row reading as 0 fails the persistence test, and a genuine 0 reading as the unknown sentinel fails its mirror. Verified live twice against a console running this build. Through the real proxy: a urlencoded form post with no query string counts 2, a JSON API post 1, a multipart upload 2, a GET with a query string 2, a GET with neither 0, and a JSON body WITH a query string 1 rather than 2 -- an unreadable body must not add to a query string that already answered. In a browser: the filter keeps all four body- and query-bearing rows and drops the genuine zero, and the hint states the count is computed server-side at capture. Screenshot at the end of the pass. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/core + internal/persist + internal/proxy + internal/web green, bun test:lib 761/0, e2e-go.sh 24/24. The committed bundle is deliberately not rebuilt: HEAD's history.tsx still calls useHistory with three arguments, which only compiles against a data.ts change another session has not committed.

internal/crawler/session_gate.go was complete and thoroughly tested -- five session-recovery tests in crawler_test.go, a fakeCoordinator, a status-flip rule, a login-page rule, a bounded re-login budget with its own stop reason, and a report that surfaces re-login health. gaps.md:1083-1092 declared it closed in 2026-08 on the strength of the mechanism. Neither production caller ever passed it: api_crawl.go:425-447 and api_apiscan.go:205-231 built their crawler.Config literals without SessionCoordinator or LoginPagePattern, so crawler.go:1260's 'if c.cfg.SessionCoordinator != nil' short-circuited on every operator-launched crawl. The consequence is the bad one: a crawl of an authenticated app follows the login redirect and reports whatever the public pages yielded, with no signal that the session had been lost. The operator gets a confident empty result and a re-run gives the same one. Both literals now carry s.crawlSessionCoordinator() and req.LoginPagePattern. It is the coordinator every other tool already routes through -- Repeater, Intruder, the proxy -- so a crawl uses the project's session handling the way Burp's crawl_using_provided_logins_only describes, and there is no second, drift-prone way to think about re-login. The API scan gets it too: it walks the same routes in a different mode, and a scan that loses its session enumerates the login redirect as though it were an endpoint. login_page_pattern is new on both request types, because the status-flip rule alone only half-closes this. An application that serves its shell with a 200 for every route -- the common SPA shape -- never flips a status, and the crawl would sit there authenticated-in-name-only. Empty keeps the status flip, so the field is optional; a malformed pattern is a 400 from crawler.New before any task row exists, which is the rule the rest of the request already follows. A pattern that silently never matched would be a control reporting a dead session as a live one. crawlSessionCoordinator returns nil for a server without a coordinator, and nil MEANS nil: a typed nil in that interface is a non-nil value holding a nil pointer, which is the shape that panics on first use rather than at the call -- worse than the original defect, because it takes the process down instead of quietly doing nothing. The two config literals are extracted into crawlConfig and apiScanConfig for a reason worth recording: my first wiring test called the helper directly and PASSED against the unwired shape. The helper was right and nothing called it, which was the entire defect. A field missing from a struct literal nobody inspects is invisible -- the same shape as the Params field's own note that 'the store kept the set, the console rendered it, the test asserted it, and the wire shape in between silently dropped it'. Reading what production actually BUILDS is the only assertion that detects this class. 8 tests, mutation-checked both ways: unwiring both literals fails 2, and a typed nil fails the real-nil test -- its message shows the trap exactly, printing <nil> for a value that is not nil. There is a behaviour test too, against a target that genuinely expires the session mid-crawl, so the claim is not only that the field is set. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/web + internal/crawler green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

A loaded Burp configuration's `crawler` object was parsed into nothing. internal/scanner/burpconfig.go reads the `scanner` half of the same file and reports every key it cannot apply; the `crawler` half -- present in 9 of Burp's 29 shipped configurations, ten keys across them (map_root.tsv:12473-12478, burp.Zmst) -- was never looked at, so a third of a shipped configuration silently did not arrive and no report line said the section had existed and been ignored. Importing a Burp configuration is a first-class migration path, and a loader that reports what it cannot honour is only honest if it looks at every section the file carries. This is the crawler's half of that, with the same three-part shape the scanner's loader already has: applied, unrepresentable, and the sections with no keys behind them at all. Burp's three shipped crawl keys all land on Limits fields this engine already has, so this is a projection and nothing more: maximum_crawl_time -> MaxDuration, maximum_unique_locations -> MaxLocations, maximum_request_count -> MaxRequests. maximum_crawl_time is SECONDS in Burp's files, and the unit is the table's fact rather than a guess at the call site: read as another unit it is a crawl whose time budget is effectively zero, which looks like 'the crawl did nothing' rather than 'the unit was misread'. A key this engine has no field for is reported by name, without the section prefix so it reads as what the operator set it under. A whole unknown SECTION is reported separately, because 'this section is gone' and 'this one key is gone' are different amounts of loss and an operator deciding whether to hand-write the difference needs to know which it is. Sections Burp's files carry but burpsy has nothing behind -- optimization among them -- are still reported: silence about them is the difference between 'your configuration said nothing' and 'your configuration said something we could not use'. The report is sorted, because Go's map iteration is random and a list that reorders itself between two reads of the same file cannot be diffed or eyeballed. Two refusals rather than two coercions. A boolean in the limits section -- Burp's limits carry numbers, its other sections booleans -- is a mistyped configuration, and coercing it to 1 gives a one-request crawl and a 'configuration applied' line. A negative limit is no limit at all, which is the thing the default limits exist to prevent. POST /api/crawl takes `config` and overlays the crawler half UNDER the explicit per-request limits, so a field the operator typed on this request still wins over the file they also named -- the other order would make a configuration silently override the request that named it. The overlay copies per field for the same reason a struct copy would be wrong: a limit the file never mentioned must not overwrite the caller's value with a zero. The reply carries config_name and config_unapplied_keys, the same not-silent half the audit path reports, because the reason an operator cannot know a third of their configuration is missing is that nothing ever said so. 9 tests, mutation-checked both ways: an unknown key silently dropped fails 2, and a loader whose loop never runs -- the field present and the code not looking at it, which is the pre-fix shape -- fails 4. Worth stating: my first attempt at the second mutation replaced the field with struct{}, which broke the build, and a build failure is not a test result. The mutation that actually models the defect compiles. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/crawler + internal/web green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

A robots.txt may name its own URL list (`Sitemap: https://x/sitemap.xml`). The crawler admitted that URL and fetched it -- then discarded the response as non-HTML at crawler.go's SkipNotHTML gate, because there was no encoding/xml anywhere in internal/crawler. A target that publishes exactly where to go had its answer fetched, stored, scanned and thrown away, and the crawl mapped only what it linked into: a confident empty result against the sites that volunteer their own structure. Burp parses it (Zgkz.java:13,18,22-24; Zb8w.java:15's SITEMAP action kind is the record of having done so). A SIBLING of the HTML gate, not a relaxation of it. isHTML exists for HTML extraction -- the link walk, form submit, base-href resolution -- and none of that applies to a sitemap; admitting XML through that gate would hand every non-HTML response to the HTML extractor looking for anchors it will never find. A PDF still records SkipNotHTML exactly as before, and a test says so. A <sitemapindex> is a sitemap OF sitemaps, so its entries are marked and re-admitted as sitemaps to fetch. A large site publishes a handful pointing at the rest, and reading only the index finds every one of them empty -- the difference between 'read one file' and 'read the list the operator published', so it is its own counter. <loc> entries enter as DISCOVERED LINKS rather than seeds, for the reason robots.txt paths do: a target-supplied URL passes the destructive-action check, the scope gate and the crawl-scope query like anything else the response contained. A sitemap naming /admin/delete-all must not become a privileged request because the target wrote it down, and a test asserts it was not fetched. The content type is a HINT and not a gate: a great many servers serve a sitemap as octet-stream or text/plain, and requiring the right header would drop the document on exactly the sites that publish one, so the body is sniffed too on the first 512 bytes for the two element names that identify the document. A failed parse is reported rather than treated as a non-sitemap, which is what makes a mislabelled sitemap recoverable instead of silent. SkipSitemapUnparsed is a new reason because the alternative IS the defect: a body that looked like a sitemap and could not be read reported as not-HTML, indistinguishable from a target that published nothing. A gzipped sitemap, a truncated fetch and a document that was never a sitemap are three facts an operator can act on differently and '0 locations' cannot tell them apart. <lastmod> is carried and not interpreted. It is what tells an operator which page changed this morning, and it is deliberately not used to order the frontier: coverage that depends on a date the target may have written wrong is coverage the crawl cannot stand behind. While adding the Skip value: skipLedger.counts was [30]uint64 hand-maintained alongside `var SkipAll = [30]Skip`, and I had the two out of step. The compiler caught SkipAll's length and NOT the counter's -- the array is only indexed at runtime, so the omission surfaced as a panic on the first decline. The counter is now [len(SkipAll)]uint64, which is the shape that cannot drift. 13 tests, mutation-checked both ways: a sitemap parsed and counted but whose locations are never admitted fails 5 (the half-fix that looks complete and finds nothing), and the branch disabled entirely -- the pre-fix shape -- fails 6. The end-to-end test seeds the ORIGIN rather than robots.txt, because the crawler asks for a seed's authority's robots.txt; seeding the file directly asserts on a path no crawl takes, and that mistake produced the one test failure here. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/crawler + internal/web green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

The config-key table reported skip_all_tests_for_parameters as `applies: false` -- 'not applied' -- while the engine HONOURED it end to end: /api/scanner/config accepts skip_all_tests_for_parameters as a list of parameter names, AuditConfig.SkipAllTestsForParameters carries it, enumerateOptions passes it to the enumerator, and bcheck's skipNamedPoints drops a matching point from every kind as a Declined. The row was false because the honoured path is a LIST-valued field and every row in the table reads through OptUint32, so the key had no shape to land in and the row said nothing. This is the honest-counting defect class the project treats as worse than a missing feature: a settings page that tells an operator their skip list is unsupported while it silently works. v9cg closed on the mechanism and jtmm fixed a build; neither fixed the lying row. But 'applied' would be the mirror-image lie, and the truth is a third thing. Burp's value is a list of MATCH RULES ({enabled, parameter, item, match_type, expression}, e.g. matches_regex over an xml_attribute name); this engine has no matcher over item or expression, so a rule that matched by expression arrives here as a name that matches nothing. So the row is now marked `partial`: BuiltInConfigKey gains Partial bool on the wire and the row struct gains listShaped beside applies, so a consumer filtering on Partial to exclude reduced-support controls from 'unsupported' can. ApplyWithReport skips a partial row rather than letting it fall through to the 'read == nil' arm that builds the unapplied list, and the what text still names exactly what is missing. Three existing tests had to move, and their failure messages are the argument: the shipped-keys test pinned TWO counts (27 applied, 28 not applied) and required every unapplied row's text to start 'not applied: '; it now pins three (27 applied in full, 1 partial, 27 not applied) and checks each bucket's prefix. Test_every_built_in_config_field_has_a_key_row enforced 'no read but claims to apply is a lie' -- which is exactly the partial state -- and now distinguishes the three combinations. The apply-overlay oracle refuses an applying key it cannot check, and skip_all_tests_for_parameters is now NAMED in that switch so the oracle covers it instead of blocking on it. Worth recording because it is silent where a compile error is not: Go accepts two struct fields carrying the SAME json tag. My first attempt gave Partial json:"applies", duplicating the field above it, so the wire carried Partial's value under Applies' name, and the struct-level tests passed because they read the Go value. The fix for that then replaced the wrong occurrence and DROPPED Applies' tag entirely, which would have renamed the field to 'Applies' on the wire. What catches either is a test that decodes the HTTP response into its own struct and asserts on the KEYS: TestEveryConfigKeyFieldReachesTheWireUnderItsOwnName. The lesson generalises -- when a wire shape is contractual, assert on the decoded response, not on the Go value. 9 tests across the two packages, mutation-checked: restoring the row to 'not applied' fails 3, and removing the ApplyWithReport guard passes until the two tests that put a preset naming the key in front of the unapplied list are added -- which is why they exist and why the mutation had to be re-run after they did. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/scanner + internal/web green, tsc clean, bun test:lib 761/0, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

Burp re-passes a FAILED audit item: number_of_follow_up_passes (Zxdx.java:27,36; shipped default 1 at Zp0d.java:120-121) drives a re-pass driver (Zeeu.java:119,239-241, Zfkz.java:57,69-81). burpsy reported the key unapplied and the dispatch loop BROKE on a failed item (audit_engine.go:1339), so a failure was final. A transient failure -- a timeout, a 502 from a backend mid-restart, a dropped connection -- permanently lost that item's coverage and was indistinguishable from a check that found nothing. The ORDER of the two steps is the whole design, and it is why the bead spells it out. A pass REPEATS the dispatch, so the narrowing lands first: without asking which checks already failed, a re-pass re-sends everything the first pass sent -- including the ones whose failure the response cannot change -- and multiplies traffic against a broken target by the number of passes. burpsy's Admit was a single bit with no failure memory, so there was nothing to consult. So the breaker now remembers, per (dispatch unit, check), which probes could not be sent: Burp's predicate asked one level coarser (Zwy6.java's Zz returns 'skip' when failedForEntireInsertionPoint < 1L, per insertion point; the dispatch plan here has (unit, check) as its granularity). Two failure sites feed it -- a check that failed before a verdict, and a check whose probes were all refused -- which are the same fact by different causes and were previously both just a counter. The loop spends a pass only when the item FAILED and some step is still retryable, which after the narrowing means some check in the item has never been tried. A budget-spent item is NOT retried: a second pass would run out of the same budget, and 'retried once' would teach an operator nothing the run's own bounds had not already said. FollowUpPasses is on AuditOutcome because a failed item that was retried and one that was not are different accounts of the same coverage loss. beginPass resets the CONSECUTIVE counters and keeps the memory, and the failed flag survives a pass. That last one is not an oversight: an item that tripped the breaker is still failed after a pass that did not clear it, and clearing the flag would make the engine's verdict depend on whether a retry HAPPENED rather than on whether the work SUCCEEDED -- so a pass that fixed nothing would report the item as merely bounded, a claim this engine does not make. The key row now applies (28 applied in full, 1 partial, 26 not applied -- the counts move, and the test says so in its failure message). Two oracle tests had to learn the new key rather than block on it, which is the guard working as intended: the shipped-keys test pins all three counts, and the apply-overlay oracle refuses an applying key it cannot check, so number_of_follow_up_passes is NAMED in that switch and checked through the resolved followUpPasses() rather than the raw OptUint32. Two of my own test assertions were inverted and said the opposite of what I meant -- that a pass clears the memory, and that it clears the failed flag. The second was a real design question I had answered wrongly before writing the code. 4 tests, mutation-checked: clearing the memory in beginPass fails the narrowing test, and a default of 0 fails the resolution test -- the latter mattering most, because an unset key resolving to 0 reads as 'no retries' and quietly disables the feature the row claims to apply. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/scanner green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

Burp's dispatch is a two-stage filter: the family switches, then a per-check predicate over the selected issue types (Zwy6.java:36-75, and lambda$isEnabled$1 at :170-184). burpsy had the first stage only, so the three selected_issues-family keys were reported unapplied and a run could not be narrowed past its families. Targeted re-audit is the ordinary operator workflow -- fix a bug, confirm the one issue class is gone -- and here it was unreachable. ScanConfig.IssueTypes is a set of catalogue type indexes, empty meaning no restriction. Type indexes rather than names because the catalogue is the identity: a name is a label, and a label an operator typed against Burp's own UI has to mean the same thing here rather than becoming a second vocabulary to keep in step. The filter is applied LAST and to BOTH sources: Burp's own order has the type filter after the family switches, so a run scoped to SQLi and path traversal can still turn the SQLi FAMILY off and select nothing of it; and it is applied to corpus entries as well as the native table, because a selection that filtered one and not the other has a hole exactly where the operator least expects one. A check with NO type index is EXCLUDED whenever a selection is in force: it is not selectable, and a selection that cannot name something must not silently keep it -- the conservative direction, since an operator asked for a set and a check they could not have chosen either way is better reported as unselected than as selected. Two paths, and only one was covered at first. enabledChecks (what a scanner LISTS) and enabledChecksUnder (what a run DISPATCHES, taking the per-run config) are different functions, and a narrowing applied only in the first is computed and discarded for every real audit. The mutation caught it: removing the filter from the audit path passed every test until TestTheSelectionNarrowsTheCheckSetAnAuditWouldDispatch exists. Same trap as nc9s, same lesson -- a test that calls the helper rather than the path a run takes cannot see an unwired seam. hasAuditLevelGate also had to learn about the selection: it answers 'does this configuration narrow the check set at all?', and a configuration that ONLY selects issue types was routed down the path that applies no narrowing -- a gate predicate written before the key existed. CheckCoverageRow gains Suppressed, and NativeCheckCoverageUnder is the selection-aware sibling. A row that is runnable and SUPPRESSED is not covered for a run under this configuration, and a coverage number that cannot say so counts it as covered -- the one thing a coverage number is for. It is distinct from a declined row (never going to run either way) and the two are asserted mutually exclusive, because two explanations for one absence is its own confusion. The three keys now apply as PARTIAL rather than in full, and the distinction is real: Burp's selected_issues value carries a per-issue enabled flag, and here the PRESENCE of a type is the enable, so the two boolean flags carry nothing beyond it. Claiming full support would be the mirror-image lie 86le is about, and the counts move to say so: 28 applied in full, 4 partial, 23 not applied. The wire gained issue_types (absent and empty are told apart by nil, because 'no selection' and 'nothing selected' are different requests) and number_of_follow_up_passes. A type index of 0 is REFUSED rather than accepted: it is not a catalogue entry, and a selection containing it would match no check at all -- an operator auditing nothing while the configuration read as a restriction. Two existing tests were pinned to the old behaviour and had to be retargeted rather than deleted, and one had stopped testing what it was written for. Test_a_parsed_unapplied_key_reaches_the_report used scan_only_selected_issues as its example of a key the parser records and the report drops; that key is honoured now, so the example cannot show the spelling hazard the test exists for (section-qualified name the parser writes vs bare name the listing looks up). It now finds its own example, matches by SUFFIX so a key moving sections cannot make it pass for the wrong reason, and asserts the mirror too: a key the engine DOES honour must not appear under either spelling. 9 tests, mutation-checked: the filter never applied fails 1, never applied on the AUDIT path fails 1, an unset selection narrowing to nothing fails 1. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/scanner + internal/web green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

Burp's rule dialog offers 18 match types per direction (burp-re/out/clean/jdt_src/burp/Zero.java:18-54, an 18-case factory; the dialog's own labels at map_root.tsv:27646-27661) and burpsy exposed seven: host, path, extension, method, url, status_code, content_type. 'Hold requests to port 8443' and 'hold the response whose body contains X' could not be written at all. Port- and protocol-scoped interception is how an operator holds one service's traffic without stopping the rest of a session, and body matching is the only way to hold the one response that matters in a high-volume stream. This adds four fields: port and protocol (both directions), request_body (requests) and response_body (responses). APPENDED, never inserted: a Field is a wire VALUE and an operator's saved rule names one, so re-numbering the existing seven would silently re-point every rule already written. A test pins the numbers for exactly that reason. The dead-weight rule the bead asks for: Direction.HasField reports whether a direction can supply a field AT ALL, and Message.FieldValue consults it before any lookup. A request has no status code, no content type and no response body, so a rule naming those in a REQUEST list matches nothing silently, and a rule that can never match is indistinguishable from a target that never sent it. The SHAPE decides, not what happens to be set on the struct: a request CARRYING a status pointer still answers "" for status_code, which is what the old shape read. The console's field list marks the per-direction fields for the same reason, and both sides read one contract rather than two that could disagree. Two robustness details a body rule needs to be worth having: bare-LF framing is read as well as CRLF, because a client that does not use CRLF is a real one and a rule that works against a hand-written fixture and never against that client reads as configured while firing on nothing; and bytes that are not an HTTP message at all -- a WebSocket frame -- supply neither half rather than answering with a fragment a rule would match on. One existing test changed rather than being papered over: TestHeld_StatusField set a status pointer on a REQUEST and expected FieldValue to return it, which is the bug this bead describes read as expected behaviour. Burp navigates with idle/quiet thresholds before it reads the DOM (Zgjj.java:161-165, map_root.tsv:7393 'Network idle threshold (ms):'). burpsy's render seam was Render func(ctx, url) (string, error) with no options and domexec slept a fixed 300 ms, so whatever the browser had at that instant WAS the page. A client-rendered route that populates after the load event contributed no links and the crawl then reported the application as having almost no locations -- a confident wrong answer, which is worse than a missing feature. Three windows, because they fail differently and an operator diagnosing a thin crawl needs to know which one bit: DOMQuiet (the DOM unchanged for N), NetworkIdle (no request in flight for N), and MaxWait (the cap). The cap is not optional -- a page with a websocket or a polling dashboard never goes quiet and would wait forever -- and it is enforced by the SAME deadline as the windows rather than by a second timer, so an unsettled page costs exactly MaxWait and not MaxWait plus a race. RenderWithOutcome is the new seam: Render plus HOW the render ended. The plain Render still works and still says nothing about settling, because a caller that wired only Render has not said it cares -- making the outcome form required would break every existing wiring for no gain. A CAPPED render's links are still admitted (they are real) and the page is also RECORDED as incomplete, naming the window it hit: 'the page never settled' and 'the browser died' are two different answers with two different remedies, and the queue has to tell them apart. Presenting a capped page as an empty one is the defect this change removes. The defaults are NON-ZERO and the number is 300 ms for a reason worth recording: that is the fixed sleep the previous implementation used unconditionally, so it is the FLOOR. My first value was 250 ms and the test caught it -- a crawl configured with nothing would have read the DOM EARLIER than it always did, which is a silent regression dressed as an improvement. The wait is now conditional, so a page that settles early returns sooner and the common case is FASTER than the old fixed sleep; 300 ms only applies to a page that keeps changing. Also: a no-DOM server hands the crawler a real nil renderer, not a function returning "". A function returning "" is a render that always produced nothing, which the engine cannot tell from a page that genuinely had none, and would report as SkipRenderUnavailable on every URL of a crawl that was never supposed to render one. 6 tests, mutation-checked: not recording the cap fails 1, and a default below the old fixed sleep fails 1. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/crawler + internal/domexec + internal/web green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.
